Lessons.Title: Predicting Populations
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: evaluate whether linear, exponential or no simple model fits measured population history; use defensible projections and discuss why extrapolation can fail. Original independently authored Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 5 Lesson 21, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/5/21/preparation.html and student tasks https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/5/21/index.html (CC BY 4.0). The publisher compares real historical city populations; these separate three first-party fictional town series are not real census evidence.

Original fictional town counts at equal decade indices t=0,1,2,3: Town A800,900,1000,1100; Town B200,300,450,675; Town C500,600,620,800. Town A has fixed difference100 each decade and a linear model A(t)=800+100t. Town B has fixed ratio1.5 and model B(t)=200(1.5)^t. Town C changes by+100,+20,+180 and ratios vary, so no single simple constant-difference or constant-ratio model matches all four points.

Extrapolating one more decade gives model A(4)=1200 and model B(4)=200(1.5)^4=1012.5; since a population is a whole-number count, report approximately1013 or a continuous proxy estimate1012.5, not a literal half person. Do not invent an extrapolation for Town C as certain just to fill a table. None of these projections is a validated forecast of real people.

Student task: compare common differences and ratios, graph all three series on shared time/population axes, decide which model fits each, propose a cautious one-step projection and explain migration, policy and sampling factors outside the model. Teacher-scored rubric0–2 each for table/graphs, model selection by evidence, correct projection and defensible limitations.

KeyConcepts.Title: Linear population pattern
KeyConcepts.Definition: A constant difference over equal decades supports a linear model.

KeyConcepts.Title: Exponential population pattern
KeyConcepts.Definition: A common successive ratio supports an exponential model.
KeyConcepts.Example: Town B grows by factor1.5 per decade.

KeyConcepts.Title: Model uncertainty
KeyConcepts.Definition: Some observed patterns do not support a unique simple trend.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Do not force a line or constant multiplier onto irregular values.

WorkedExamples.Method: Work from the explicitly fictional data and verify the original model, units and domain.
Steps: Neither exact linear nor exact fixed-factor exponential model matches all four.
Collect more context before choosing a forecast.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No simple exact linear or exponential pattern for C.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Calling an extrapolated population prediction a measured census result
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The next decade has not been observed and data are fictional.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reporting half a person as an exact headcount
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The real-number model produces fractional outputs.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Forcing irregular history to a constant-ratio expression
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Different ratios disprove that exact assumption.

SummaryPoints: Repeated differences and ratios help choose plausible model classes.
Town A is linear, B exponential, C neither under exact simple patterns.
One-step projections are conditional, not guaranteed real populations.
Teacher scores original graphs and uncertainty arguments.
